title: YOU CANNOT UNDERSTAND THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT WITHOUT READING ABOUT THE WORKS OF THE FLESH
paragraphs: YOU CANNOT UNDERSTAND THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT WITHOUT READING ABOUT THE WORKS OF THE FLESH

Everybody wants the fruit of the Spirit. But few are willing to confront the flesh that keeps resisting the Spirit. What if the greatest evidence of your spiritual growth is not how loudly you worship, but what happens inside you when nobody is watching?
You can raise your hands during worship and still use those same hands to type words that destroy another person.
You can memorize Scripture and still secretly celebrate the downfall of someone you envy.
You can preach about forgiveness while rehearsing the offenses of people who hurt you.
You can post about the goodness of God in the morning and surrender to temptation before midnight.
You can look spiritually alive in public while privately feeding the very things Christ calls you to crucify.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you can become so accustomed to this contradiction that it no longer bothers you.
We love reading about love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
We print them on shirts. We write them in journals. We display them inside our homes. We preach about them, pray for them, and proudly share them on social media.
But immediately before the Apostle Paul describes the fruit of the Spirit, he exposes something considerably more uncomfortable.
The works of the flesh.
And there is a reason these two realities appear together in Galatians 5.
Paul was not simply giving Christians a beautiful collection of virtues to admire. He was revealing a spiritual conflict that every believer must confront.
A conflict between what our fallen desires demand and what the Holy Spirit produces.
Between self-gratification and surrender.
Between the life we once lived and the life Christ is forming within us.
Between the person we desperately want others to believe we are and the person God knows we actually are.
Galatians 5:16–17 declares:

“This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other.” — KJV
The original Greek of Galatians 5:16 begins with:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε — Pneumati peripateite.
Literally, “Walk by the Spirit.”
The Greek verb peripateite (περιπατεῖτε) is a present imperative. In this context, walking describes an ongoing manner of living rather than merely a single spiritual experience.
Paul is not telling us to visit the presence of God occasionally.
He is calling us to live under the direction of the Holy Spirit continually.
Not merely on Sundays.
Not merely when the worship music moves us.
Not merely when life becomes unbearable and we suddenly remember how to pray.
But when someone insults us.
When nobody would discover our dishonesty.
When temptation presents itself in the privacy of our bedrooms.
When our pride is wounded.
When someone receives the blessing we have been praying for.
When obedience costs us something we desperately want to keep.
That is where walking by the Spirit becomes more than religious vocabulary.
That is where discipleship becomes painfully personal.
Before Paul describes the fruit, he writes in Galatians 5:19:
φανερὰ δέ ἐστιν τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός — Phanera de estin ta erga tēs sarkos.
“Now the works of the flesh are evident.”
The word erga (ἔργα) means works, deeds, or actions.
The word sarx (σάρξ), translated as “flesh,” can refer to physical flesh in other contexts. Here, however, Paul uses it to describe fallen human existence and desires in opposition to God's Spirit.
He is not teaching that the human body itself is inherently evil. Scripture teaches that our bodies belong to God and are to glorify Him (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
The problem is sin operating within fallen humanity.
It is the human inclination to live independently of God, enthroning our desires above His will.

Paul then identifies the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:19–21: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, hostility, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish rivalries, divisions, factions, envy, drunkenness, wild revelry, and things like these.
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because somewhere in that passage, there may be something we have learned to excuse.
We condemn sexual immorality but tolerate jealousy.
We condemn drunkenness but justify our uncontrollable anger.
We condemn idolatry but build our entire identity around money, reputation, relationships, influence, or the approval of others.
We condemn sorcery but entertain bitterness.
We condemn public scandals but privately participate in gossip, rivalry, division, and character assassination.
We become experts at recognizing the flesh in other people while remaining remarkably creative at renaming it within ourselves.
We call pride confidence.
We call jealousy discernment.
We call cruelty honesty.
We call revenge justice.
We call gossip concern.
We call selfish ambition purpose.
We call uncontrolled anger personality.
And sometimes, we even use Scripture to defend the very attitudes Scripture commands us to abandon.
The flesh does not become holy simply because it learns how to speak Christian.
One of the most disturbing realities about Galatians 5 is that many of the works Paul identifies can operate inside religious communities.
Hostility can exist inside a church.
Jealousy can exist inside a ministry.
Selfish ambition can exist behind a pulpit.
Division can exist among people who sing the same worship songs.
Envy can hide behind a prayer request.
A person can defend correct doctrine while displaying a deeply unchristlike character.
Truth matters. Sound doctrine matters. Biblical conviction matters.
But the truth we profess must also confront the sin we practice.
Paul himself warned the Galatians:
“But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.” — Galatians 5:15
These words were addressed to people within the Christian community.
Imagine that.
People who had heard the Gospel of grace were in danger of destroying one another.
They needed more than theological arguments.
They needed to walk by the Spirit.
Perhaps you know what this feels like.
Perhaps someone wounded you so deeply that you began to enjoy imagining their downfall.
Perhaps you have spent years comparing your life with someone else's, wondering why God seems to bless them while you remain in the same painful season.
Perhaps your marriage is suffering because your anger keeps speaking before your love does.
Perhaps your children have heard more of your frustration than your encouragement.
Perhaps your private internet history tells a different story from your public testimony.
Perhaps you are exhausted from repeatedly promising God that you will never return to the same sin, only to find yourself returning again.
Perhaps nobody knows how much you are struggling.
But God knows.
And the remarkable thing about the Gospel is that the God who sees everything is also the God who calls you to come into the light.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Not because holiness is optional.
But because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Paul does not soften the seriousness of the works of the flesh.
At the end of Galatians 5:21, he warns:
“They which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.”
The Greek expression is:
οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες — Hoi ta toiauta prassontes.
“Those who practice such things.”
The present participle prassontes describes those engaged in such conduct. In the context of Paul's teaching, this is a serious warning against a life characterized by the works of the flesh.
It does not mean that a Christian who stumbles once is automatically beyond redemption.
Nor does it mean that struggling against temptation proves you have no relationship with God.
Galatians 6:1 explicitly instructs spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in a transgression with gentleness.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
But neither passage gives us permission to make peace with sin.
There is a profound difference between falling into sin and defending sin as your rightful way of life.
Between grieving over your rebellion and celebrating it.
Between struggling against temptation and deliberately building a home for it.
Repentance does not mean you have achieved sinless perfection. It means you are turning toward God rather than insisting that your rebellion deserves His approval.
And then, after exposing the works of the flesh, Paul introduces one of the most beautiful contrasts in Scripture.
ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη, μακροθυμία, χρηστότης, ἀγαθωσύνη, πίστις, πραΰτης, ἐγκράτεια.
Ho de karpos tou pneumatos estin agapē, chara, eirēnē, makrothymia, chrēstotēs, agathōsynē, pistis, prautēs, enkrateia.
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” — Galatians 5:22–23, translation from the Greek
Notice something remarkable.
Paul speaks of the works of the flesh using the plural erga, but the fruit of the Spirit using the singular karpos (καρπός).

Fruit can function as a collective noun, and the singular alone does not establish an entire theological doctrine. Nevertheless, Paul's contrast beautifully presents these qualities together as the produce of the Spirit's work.
They are not nine independent spiritual trophies we collect to prove our superiority.
They describe the character the Holy Spirit cultivates in those who belong to Christ.
And suddenly, the works of the flesh help us appreciate the significance of every quality Paul names.
Love — ἀγάπη (agapē) — confronts our hostility, jealousy, and selfishness.
It seeks the good of others rather than treating people as instruments for personal gratification.
It does not require us to approve of sin or remain in abusive situations. Biblical love rejoices with the truth (1 Corinthians 13:6).
But it refuses to make hatred its home.
Love becomes visible when you stop allowing another person's wrongdoing to determine your character.
Joy — χαρά (chara) — confronts the endless hunger of a heart that believes satisfaction can only come through getting what it wants.
Christian joy is not pretending that suffering does not hurt.
Paul experienced imprisonment, rejection, hardship, and grief. Yet he could still speak of rejoicing in the Lord.
Joy is not the absence of tears.
It is the presence of hope even when the tears will not stop.
Peace — εἰρήνη (eirēnē) — confronts hostility, strife, and division.
It does not mean avoiding every difficult conversation or compromising biblical truth to keep everyone comfortable.
It means refusing to become a willing servant of unnecessary conflict.
Through Christ, believers have peace with God (Romans 5:1), and that reconciliation shapes how we pursue peace with others.
Sometimes peace looks like putting down your phone instead of sending the message you know will cause another war.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing without adding an excuse.
Sometimes it looks like establishing a necessary boundary without allowing bitterness to consume you.
Patience — μακροθυμία (makrothymia) — confronts our outbursts of anger and our unwillingness to endure inconvenience, frustration, or offense.
The word carries the sense of patience, forbearance, and long-suffering.
It is the capacity to endure provocation without immediately retaliating.
Think about the people who have had to endure your imperfections.
Think about the patience God has shown you.
How many times has He confronted your rebellion, called you back, and extended mercy when you deserved judgment?
Remembering the patience of God changes the way we respond to imperfect people.
Kindness — χρηστότης (chrēstotēs) — confronts cruelty, harshness, and indifference.
Kindness is not weakness.
It is goodness expressed through the way we treat others.
It is possible to speak biblical truth without humiliating the person who needs to hear it.
Romans 2:4 reminds us that God's kindness is intended to lead people to repentance.
How tragic when Christians use the truth of God as an excuse to display the cruelty of their flesh.
Goodness — ἀγαθωσύνη (agathōsynē) — confronts moral corruption and the pursuit of selfish pleasure.
Goodness is more than maintaining a respectable appearance.
It is moral uprightness expressed through a life increasingly aligned with God's will.
It is returning what does not belong to you.
It is refusing dishonest profit.
It is doing what is right when doing wrong would be easier, more profitable, and completely hidden from human eyes.
Faithfulness — πίστις (pistis) — confronts instability, betrayal, and divided loyalties.
The Greek word can mean faith, trust, or faithfulness depending on context. Within this list, faithfulness is a widely accepted rendering.
It describes reliability and fidelity.
It is remaining trustworthy when circumstances change.
It is honoring commitments when emotions fade.
It is continuing to follow Jesus when obedience no longer feels exciting.
Faithfulness is not measured only by the intensity of your worship during a spiritual breakthrough, but also by your willingness to obey God in the ordinary days that follow.
Gentleness — πραΰτης (prautēs) — confronts aggression, arrogance, and the desire to dominate.
Biblical gentleness is not cowardice or moral compromise.
Jesus described Himself as gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29), yet He never surrendered the truth.
Gentleness allows you to correct without unnecessarily crushing.
To confront without humiliating.
To possess authority without abusing it.
To recognize that another person's weakness is not an opportunity to demonstrate your superiority.
Self-control — ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia) — confronts the tyranny of unchecked desires.
Sexual immorality, drunkenness, uncontrolled anger, and other destructive indulgences reveal what happens when desires become masters rather than servants.
Self-control does not mean temptation disappears.
It means temptation is no longer entitled to your obedience.
You may feel the desire to return to pornography.
You may feel the desire to retaliate.
You may feel the desire to drink beyond sobriety, indulge resentment, or satisfy an appetite that is destroying you.
But by God's grace, your desires do not have to dictate your decisions.

And sometimes the Spirit-led decision is intensely practical: deleting an application, ending an inappropriate relationship, seeking accountability, receiving professional help, confessing hidden sin, or removing yourself from an environment that repeatedly draws you into temptation.
Do you see why we must read the works of the flesh before celebrating the fruit of the Spirit?
Because the fruit becomes profoundly personal when we recognize what it stands against.
Love means something different when hatred has been consuming you.
Peace means something different when your home has become a battlefield.
Patience means something different when your anger has wounded the people you love.
Faithfulness means something different when betrayal has become your secret.
Self-control means something different when your appetites have been controlling your life.
The fruit of the Spirit is not decorative Christianity.
It is evidence of the Spirit's transforming work.
But here is where we must be extremely careful.
The Gospel is not a self-improvement program.
Jesus did not die merely to make unpleasant people more pleasant.
He died for our sins and rose again, accomplishing what we could never accomplish through our own moral efforts (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The context of Galatians is essential.
Paul was confronting teaching that pressured Gentile believers to receive circumcision and rely upon works of the law as necessary for justification.
He had already declared in Galatians 2:16 that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.
The fruit of the Spirit cannot be separated from that Gospel foundation.
We are not saved because we successfully produce enough spiritual fruit.
We are saved by God's grace through faith, and that grace leads us into a transformed life.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes this beautifully clear: salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works, yet believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The fruit is not the price of salvation. It is the evidence of a life being transformed by the One who saves.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.”
A branch cannot produce living fruit by pretending to be connected to the vine.
It must receive its life from the vine.
In the same way, Christianity is not merely learning how to imitate the outward appearance of holiness while remaining inwardly independent of Christ.
It is abiding in Him.
Depending upon Him.
Trusting Him.
Receiving His Word.
Obeying His commands.
Walking by His Spirit.
And returning to Him in repentance when we fall.
The Christian life involves real effort, real obedience, and real resistance against sin. But it is never an independent achievement of human righteousness.
Philippians 2:12–13 holds these truths together: believers are called to obedience because God Himself works within them, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.
Grace does not eliminate obedience.
Grace makes obedience possible and gives it a different foundation.
We obey not to purchase God's love, but in response to the love He has demonstrated through Christ.
Then comes the verse that many people conveniently stop reading before they reach.
Galatians 5:24:
“And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”
The Greek word translated “crucified” is ἐσταύρωσαν — estaurōsan, from stauroō, meaning to crucify.
Paul deliberately uses the language of the cross.

Those who belong to Christ have decisively broken with the flesh's rightful claim to rule their lives. Yet the surrounding commands to walk by the Spirit show that believers must continue living consistently with that reality.
There is no promise here that temptation will immediately disappear.
There is a declaration that the flesh no longer has legitimate authority over those who belong to Jesus.
You cannot nurture rebellion and call it spiritual maturity.
You cannot continually defend what Christ calls you to surrender and expect that contradiction to remain spiritually harmless.
You cannot demand that Jesus bless the very chains He came to break.
And perhaps that is why this passage feels so uncomfortable.
We want resurrection without surrender.
We want transformation without repentance.
We want the comfort of forgiveness without confronting the sin that requires forgiveness.
We want Jesus to heal the consequences while leaving our favorite compromises untouched.
But Jesus loves us too deeply to affirm everything that is destroying us.
The same Savior who receives sinners also calls them to repentance.
The same Savior who forgives also calls His disciples to follow Him.
The same grace that rescues us teaches us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions (Titus 2:11–12).
And this is where scandal meets grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted the church.
The Corinthians had backgrounds marked by serious sexual and moral sins.
Yet the Gospel was not powerless against their past.
Paul writes to the Corinthians after describing various sinful ways of life:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11
Such were some of you.
What a beautiful declaration of redemption.
Your history is not beyond the reach of Christ.
The worst chapter of your life does not have to become the defining chapter of your eternity.
The anger that characterized your past does not have to govern your future.
The sexual sin you are ashamed of does not place you beyond the invitation to repent.
The addiction you have struggled with does not make seeking freedom pointless.
The bitterness you have carried for years does not have to accompany you into every remaining season of your life.
Jesus Christ is not merely interested in improving your reputation.
He came to redeem you.
And redemption reaches deeper than reputation ever could.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heavy heart because you recognize more of the works of the flesh in your life than you wanted to admit.
Do not respond by pretending.
Do not respond by comparing yourself with someone whose sins appear worse.
And do not confuse conviction with a declaration that you are beyond hope.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Bring your sin into the light.
Confess it before God.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Pursue accountability.
Return to Scripture.
Pray when you feel strong, and pray when you feel spiritually exhausted.
Do not wait until you feel worthy to come to Jesus.
Your worthiness was never the foundation of His invitation.
His mercy is.
And when you fail, do not use grace as permission to remain where you fell.
Let grace lead you back to Christ.
Spiritual maturity is not demonstrated by claiming you have nothing left to repent of.
It becomes visible as you increasingly recognize sin, resist it, confess it, and depend upon Christ rather than defending yourself.
Maybe today your greatest spiritual victory will not be preaching to thousands.
Maybe it will be apologizing to your spouse.
Maybe it will be confessing something you have hidden for years.
Maybe it will be refusing to participate in another conversation that destroys someone's reputation.
Maybe it will be celebrating the success of someone you once envied.
Maybe it will be choosing sobriety, seeking help, forgiving an offender, or finally admitting that you cannot overcome this struggle through willpower alone.
These moments may never receive applause.
Nobody may post about them.
Nobody may know what obedience cost you.
But your Father sees what happens in secret.
And the quiet work of the Holy Spirit is not insignificant simply because it happens outside the spotlight.
Let those words be more than a comment.
Let them express a genuine prayer.

There may be someone among your friends, relatives, coworkers, or followers who is quietly fighting a battle nobody knows about. Sharing biblical encouragement is one practical way you can help bring the truth of Scripture into places we might never reach ourselves.
The world already has enough voices telling people to follow every desire of their hearts.
We need more voices pointing hearts toward Jesus.
Scripture recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while also emphasizing that giving must come willingly from the heart.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
But voluntary generosity can be a meaningful expression of gratitude to God and a practical way of helping Gospel-centered work continue.
Because the goal is not to build a community of people who merely look religious.
It is to encourage people to become faithful disciples of Jesus.
People who love when hatred would be easier.
People who pursue peace when revenge feels justified.
People who remain faithful when compromise becomes convenient.
People who repent when pride demands an excuse.
People whose private lives increasingly reflect the Savior they publicly proclaim.
So tonight, when the noise settles and nobody is watching, ask yourself something more important than whether other people consider you a good Christian.
What am I allowing to grow within me?
What am I secretly feeding?
What am I still defending that Scripture calls me to surrender?
And does the way I treat people reveal the character of the Christ I claim to follow?
Galatians 5:25 leaves us with this invitation:
“If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.”
The Greek word used for walking here is stoichōmen (στοιχῶμεν), carrying the sense of keeping in step or living in accordance with something.
If the Spirit is the source of our new life, our conduct should increasingly follow His direction.
Not perfectly through our own strength.
But faithfully through dependence upon Christ.
There is still grace for the repentant.
There is still forgiveness for the confessing sinner.
There is still hope for the exhausted believer.
There is still mercy for the person who has fallen and is turning back toward Jesus.
The cross remains the place where our pride is confronted, our sin is exposed, our forgiveness is secured, and our hope is restored.
Do not merely admire the fruit.
Do not merely condemn the flesh in others.
Abide in Christ.
Walk by the Spirit.
And surrender what you have spent so long trying to protect.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not that you never had a scandalous past, but that your past encountered a Savior whose grace was greater than your sin.
May the people who once knew the damage your flesh could cause one day encounter the beauty that Christ's Spirit has cultivated within you.
